paragraphs.heading: A land plant in the sea
paragraphs.text: Seagrasses are the one group of land plants that grows in the sea. Their ancestors lived on land and moved back into the ocean somewhere between 70 and 100 million years ago. The name comes from their long, narrow leaves. Many species spread outward as their rhizomes extend, forming wide meadows that look a lot like grassland.

paragraphs.heading: Where they grow
paragraphs.text: Like every plant that makes its own food, seagrasses photosynthesize, so they live in water that sunlight reaches. Most grow in shallow, sheltered coastal water, anchored in sand or mud. There are only about 60 fully marine species, yet they have spread across the continental shelves of every continent except Antarctica. Where they do well, they form dense meadows that rank among the most productive ecosystems on Earth.

paragraphs.heading: Pollen that hitches a ride
paragraphs.text: Most species are pollinated under water and complete their whole life cycle there, and their seeds are made under water too. Scientists long assumed that drifting currents alone carried the pollen. At least one species, Thalassia testudinum, proved otherwise: crabs and the larvae of polychaete worms have been found carrying its pollen. Rather than offering nectar like flowers on land, the plant makes sticky, nourishing clumps of pollen that draw these animals in and cling to them.

paragraphs.heading: Built for life under water
paragraphs.text: Seagrass leaves have a reduced cuticle, and their outer skin has no stomata while doing most of the photosynthesis. The roots can survive where there is no oxygen, relying on oxygen carried down from the leaves and rhizomes, and they also help move nutrients. Genome studies show that on the return to the sea some genes were lost, such as those for stomata. The make-up of the plants' cell walls also changed in radical ways.

paragraphs.heading: Why the meadows matter
paragraphs.text: Seagrass meadows act as important carbon sinks. They feed and shelter a variety of sea life that compares with coral reefs. Many creatures use them as places to breed and raise young, and they help commercial fisheries. More broadly, seagrasses strongly shape the physical, chemical and biological conditions of coastal waters.

paragraphs.heading: A shrinking habitat
paragraphs.text: Several studies point to seagrass habitat declining around the world. Ten species, 14% of all seagrasses, face a raised risk of extinction, and three of them count as endangered. Losing these meadows would hurt marine life and the people who depend on the resources and services that seagrasses provide.
